claim: MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors are involved in synchronizing circadian rhythms.
source: Melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2 are involved in synchronizing circadian rhythms and are important targets for treating sleep and mood disorders, type-2 diabetes and cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background claim about MT receptors.

claim: MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors are important targets for treating sleep and mood disorders, type-2 diabetes and cancer.
source: Melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2 are involved in synchronizing circadian rhythms and are important targets for treating sleep and mood disorders, type-2 diabetes and cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general background claim about MT receptors.

claim: Large scale structure-based virtual screening was performed using recently solved high-resolution 3D crystal structures of agonist-bound MT receptors.
source: Here, we performed large scale structure-based virtual screening for new ligand chemotypes using recently solved high-resolution 3D crystal structures of agonist-bound MT receptors.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Experimental testing of 62 screening candidates yielded the discovery of 10 new agonist chemotypes with sub-micromolar potency at MT receptors.
source: Experimental testing of 62 screening candidates yielded the discovery of 10 new agonist chemotypes with sub-micromolar potency at MT receptors, with compound 21 reaching EC50 of 0.36 nM.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental work reported in the study.

claim: Compound 21 has an EC50 of 0.36 nM at MT receptors.
source: Experimental testing of 62 screening candidates yielded the discovery of 10 new agonist chemotypes with sub-micromolar potency at MT receptors, with compound 21 reaching EC50 of 0.36 nM.
evidence: This is a specific experimental result for compound 21.

claim: Six of the discovered molecules displayed selectivity for MT2 over MT1.
source: Six of these molecules displayed selectivity for MT2 over MT1.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental characterization of the hits.

claim: Compounds 21 and 28 had dramatically reduced arrestin recruitment at MT2.
source: Moreover, two most potent agonists, including 21 and a close derivative of melatonin, 28, had dramatically reduced arrestin recruitment at MT2, while compound 37 was devoid of Gi signaling at MT1, implying biased signaling.
evidence: This is an experimental finding about the signaling properties of these compounds.

claim: Compound 37 was devoid of Gi signaling at MT1.
source: Moreover, two most potent agonists, including 21 and a close derivative of melatonin, 28, had dramatically reduced arrestin recruitment at MT2, while compound 37 was devoid of Gi signaling at MT1, implying biased signaling.
evidence: This is an experimental finding about the signaling properties of compound 37.

claim: The differential signaling profiles of compounds 21, 28, and 37 imply biased signaling.
source: Moreover, two most potent agonists, including 21 and a close derivative of melatonin, 28, had dramatically reduced arrestin recruitment at MT2, while compound 37 was devoid of Gi signaling at MT1, implying biased signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on differential signaling.

claim: This study validates the suitability of the agonist-bound orthosteric pocket in the MT receptor structures for the structure-based discovery of selective agonists.
source: This study validates the suitability of the agonist-bound orthosteric pocket in the MT receptor structures for the structure-based discovery of selective agonists.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful discovery of agonists using the crystal structures.

claim: Melatonin is found in all mammals, including humans.
source: Melatonin is found in all mammals, including humans, where it regulates sleep and helps to synchronize the circadian rhythm with natural light-dark cycles (Brzezinski, 1997; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Melatonin regulates sleep and helps to synchronize the circadian rhythm with natural light-dark cycles.
source: Melatonin is found in all mammals, including humans, where it regulates sleep and helps to synchronize the circadian rhythm with natural light-dark cycles (Brzezinski, 1997; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Melatonin is synthesized from serotonin in the pineal gland of the brain during darkness.
source: Chemically, melatonin is synthesized from serotonin in the pineal gland of the brain during darkness (Ganguly et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Both MT1 and MT2 share canonical helical 7-transmembrane (7-TM) topology.
source: Both MT1 and MT2 share canonical helical 7-transmembrane (7-TM) topology (Johansson et al., 2019; Stauch et al., 2019), although they are differentially expressed and implicated in diverse biological functions and pathologies (Dubocovich and Markowska, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature including the crystal structures.

claim: MT1 and MT2 are differentially expressed and implicated in diverse biological functions and pathologies.
source: Both MT1 and MT2 share canonical helical 7-transmembrane (7-TM) topology (Johansson et al., 2019; Stauch et al., 2019), although they are differentially expressed and implicated in diverse biological functions and pathologies (Dubocovich and Markowska, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Ramelteon has been approved for primary chronic insomnia treatment.
source: While exogenous melatonin has been commonly used for the treatment of insomnia and jetlag, more effective and long-lasting MT agonists such as ramelteon have been approved for primary chronic insomnia treatment, because of their low side-effect profile as compared to other sleeping aids such as benzodiazepines (Hardeland et al., 2011; Erman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ramelteon has a low side-effect profile compared to other sleeping aids such as benzodiazepines.
source: While exogenous melatonin has been commonly used for the treatment of insomnia and jetlag, more effective and long-lasting MT agonists such as ramelteon have been approved for primary chronic insomnia treatment, because of their low side-effect profile as compared to other sleeping aids such as benzodiazepines (Hardeland et al., 2011; Erman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tasimelteon is used for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorders in blind individuals.
source: Other MT agonists such as tasimelteon and agomelatine, are used for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorders in blind individuals and as an atypical anti-depressant for major depressive disorders, respectively (Lavedan et al., 2015; de Bodinat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Agomelatine is used as an atypical anti-depressant for major depressive disorders.
source: Other MT agonists such as tasimelteon and agomelatine, are used for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorders in blind individuals and as an atypical anti-depressant for major depressive disorders, respectively (Lavedan et al., 2015; de Bodinat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MT receptors play an essential role in learning, memory, and neuroprotection.
source: Recent studies also suggest MT receptors play an essential role in learning, memory, and neuroprotection (Liu et al., 2016) and illustrate the potential utility of partial and selective MT2 receptor agonists as antinociceptive drugs (López-Canul et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Partial and selective MT2 receptor agonists have potential utility as antinociceptive drugs.
source: Recent studies also suggest MT receptors play an essential role in learning, memory, and neuroprotection (Liu et al., 2016) and illustrate the potential utility of partial and selective MT2 receptor agonists as antinociceptive drugs (López-Canul et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MT2 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are implicated in type-2 diabetes.
source: Moreover, MT2 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are implicated in type-2 diabetes (Karamitri et al., 2018) (T2D), emphasizing the importance of MT receptors in a wide variety of functions relevant to human health and the quality of life (Karamitri and Jockers, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Most of the currently available drugs non-selectively activate both MT1 and MT2 receptors.
source: Although MT1 and MT2 receptors have distinctive in vivo functions, most of the currently available drugs non-selectively activate both MT1 and MT2 receptors (Zlotos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The MT2 receptor regulates non-rapid eye movement (NREM) while MT1 mediates rapid eye movement (REM) phases of the vigilance state in sleep architecture.
source: For example, the MT2 receptor regulates non-rapid eye movement (NREM) while MT1 mediates rapid eye movement (REM) phases of the vigilance state in sleep architecture (Comai et al., 2013; Fisher and Sugden, 2009; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The three-dimensional structures of MT1 and MT2 were determined using an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL).
source: Recently, the three-dimensional structures of MT1 and MT2 were determined using an X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL), providing atomic-level details of receptor-ligand interactions (Johansson et al., 2019; Stauch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both MT1 and MT2 receptors were resolved in complexes with agonists – agomelatine, 2-phenylmelatonin, 2-iodomelatonin and ramelteon.
source: Although both receptors were resolved in complexes with agonists – agomelatine, 2-phenylmelatonin, 2-iodomelatonin and ramelteon, thermostabilizing mutations that were necessary for crystallization rendered these receptors functionally inactive.
evidence: This describes the ligands co-crystallized with the receptors.

claim: Thermostabilizing mutations that were necessary for crystallization rendered MT1 and MT2 receptors functionally inactive.
source: Although both receptors were resolved in complexes with agonists – agomelatine, 2-phenylmelatonin, 2-iodomelatonin and ramelteon, thermostabilizing mutations that were necessary for crystallization rendered these receptors functionally inactive.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the crystallized receptors.

claim: A library of 8.4 million available-for-purchase fragment-like and lead-like compounds was used for virtual ligand screening.
source: Here, we utilized the MT structural information to perform a large scale virtual ligand screen (VLS) on both MT1 and MT2 receptors, using libraries of 8.4 million available-for-purchase fragment-like and lead-like compounds (Sterling and Irwin, 2015).
evidence: This describes the screening library used in the study.

claim: Five hits were partial agonists at MT2.
source: Six of these hits, including the most potent one, demonstrated selectivity for MT2, while five hits were partial agonists at MT2.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental characterization of the hits.

claim: Compound 21 shows substantial bias towards G-protein signaling at MT2.
source: Moreover, the two most potent MT2 compounds, 21 and a close derivative of melatonin, 28, show reduced arrestin signaling, thus resulting in substantial bias towards G-protein signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on signaling bias.

claim: Compound 28 shows substantial bias towards G-protein signaling at MT2.
source: Moreover, the two most potent MT2 compounds, 21 and a close derivative of melatonin, 28, show reduced arrestin signaling, thus resulting in substantial bias towards G-protein signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on signaling bias.

claim: The optimized models of MT receptors showed substantial improvement in AUC values over the crystal structures.
source: The AUC values for the optimized models of MT receptors showed substantial improvement over AUC values for MT crystal structures (MT1_Opt = 87 vs. MT1_Xtal = 69; and MT2_Opt = 82 vs. MT2_Xtal = 70) (see Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a result from the benchmarking analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The major interactions in MT receptor binding include aromatic stacking of the heterocyclic core with ECL2 hydrophobic residue F179/192ECL2.
source: The major interactions include aromatic stacking of the heterocyclic core with ECL2 hydrophobic residue F179/192ECL2 (the residue numbers for MT1 and MT2 listed for UniProt (Bateman et al., 2017) ids: P48039 and P49286, respectively, followed by superscripted Ballesteros – Weinstein numbering scheme Ballesteros and Weinstein, 1995), as well as hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60 and Q181/194ECL2 (Johansson et al., 2019; Stauch et al., 2019) .
evidence: This is supported by citations to the crystal structures.

claim: The major interactions in MT receptor binding include hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60 and Q181/194ECL2.
source: The major interactions include aromatic stacking of the heterocyclic core with ECL2 hydrophobic residue F179/192ECL2 (the residue numbers for MT1 and MT2 listed for UniProt (Bateman et al., 2017) ids: P48039 and P49286, respectively, followed by superscripted Ballesteros – Weinstein numbering scheme Ballesteros and Weinstein, 1995), as well as hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60 and Q181/194ECL2 (Johansson et al., 2019; Stauch et al., 2019) .
evidence: This is supported by citations to the crystal structures.

claim: A final set of 62 compounds were selected for purchase based on a multidimensional composite criterion.
source: A final set of 62 compounds (23 from only MT1 VLS; 25 from only MT2 VLS; 14 from both MT1 and MT2 VLS) were selected for purchase based on a multidimensional composite criterion accounting for compound novelty, chemical diversity, well-defined interaction patterns with binding site residues N162/1754.60 and/or Q181/194ECL2, and interaction similarities with ligands observed in the crystal structures (See Figure 2; Supplementary file 1 Table S1).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for experimental testing.

claim: Most of the compounds represented new chemotypes with Tanimoto chemical distance values >0.22.
source: Most of the compounds represented new chemotypes with Tanimoto chemical distance values >0.22 (Abagyan et al., 2016), separating them from known high-affinity MT ligands available in CHEMBL24 (Gaulton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from the chemical similarity analysis.

claim: Compound 28 is a close analog of melatonin with Tanimoto distance = 0.05.
source: We also chose a close analog of melatonin – compound 28 (Tanimoto distance = 0.05), which to our knowledge, has not yet been characterized as a ligand for MT receptors (Gaulton et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the chemical similarity of compound 28 to melatonin.

claim: Eleven compounds demonstrated sub-micromolar potencies in Gi/o mediated signaling assays (18% hit rate).
source: Eleven compounds (Table 1; Figure 3) demonstrated sub-micromolar potencies in Gi/o mediated signaling assays (18% hit rate).
evidence: This is a primary result from the experimental testing.

claim: Ten of the eleven active compounds showed binding affinities Ki <10 µM in a competition binding assay.
source: Ten of these eleven compounds also showed binding affinities Ki <10 µM in a competition binding assay (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the binding assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compound 28 was as potent as melatonin itself in MT2 (EC50 = 0.04 nM).
source: The melatonin derivative 28 identified by VLS was as potent as melatonin itself in MT2 (EC50 = 0.04 nM) and had the same potency (EC50 = 0.04 nM) at MT1.
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 28.

claim: Compound 28 had the same potency (EC50 = 0.04 nM) at MT1 as at MT2.
source: The melatonin derivative 28 identified by VLS was as potent as melatonin itself in MT2 (EC50 = 0.04 nM) and had the same potency (EC50 = 0.04 nM) at MT1.
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 28.

claim: Compound 21 displayed an EC50 = 0.36 nM for MT2, with a 30-fold selectivity over MT1 receptor (MT1 EC50 = 12 nM).
source: The most potent new chemotype, 21, displayed an EC50 = 0.36 nM for MT2, with a 30-fold selectivity over MT1 receptor (MT1EC50 = 12 nM).
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 21.

claim: Seven hits had EC50 <100 nM for at least one of the melatonin receptors.
source: Overall, seven hits had EC50 <100 nM for at least one of the melatonin receptors.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: Most of the hits identified belong to a library of fragment-like compounds with molecular weights less than 250 Da.
source: Similar to other low molecular weight MT ligands, most of the hits identified belong to a library of fragment-like compounds with molecular weights less than 250 Da, and have exceptionally high ligand efficiency (LE), far exceeding the ~0.3 value considered as a standard for a promising lead.
evidence: This describes the properties of the hit compounds.

claim: Compound 21 had the highest LE values of 0.83 kcal/mol per non-hydrogen atom for MT2 and 0.69 kcal/mol per non-hydrogen atom for MT1 receptors.
source: For example, compound 21 (Mol. Wt. = 224 Da) had the highest LE values of 0.83 kcal/mol per non-hydrogen atom for MT2 and 0.69 kcal/mol per non-hydrogen atom for MT1 receptors (Hopkins et al., 2004; Hopkins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 21.

claim: Nine out of eleven hits have methoxy or a similar group predicted to make hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60.
source: Nine out of eleven hits have methoxy or a similar group predicted to make hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60, which was found to be a critical residue for receptor activation, despite playing a limited role in ligand affinity or structural stability of the receptor (Stauch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the docking analysis.

claim: N162/1754.60 was found to be a critical residue for receptor activation.
source: Nine out of eleven hits have methoxy or a similar group predicted to make hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60, which was found to be a critical residue for receptor activation, despite playing a limited role in ligand affinity or structural stability of the receptor (Stauch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Seven of the hits were predicted to form hydrogen bonding interactions with Q181/194ECL2 similar to alkylamide tail of melatonin.
source: Furthermore, seven of the hits were predicted to form hydrogen bonding interactions with Q181/194ECL2 similar to alkylamide tail of melatonin.
evidence: This is a result from the docking analysis.

claim: Five hits were predicted to occupy a significant space in the pocket flanked by TMs-II, III, and VII forming hydrophobic interactions, especially with residues Y281/2947.38 and Y285/2987.43.
source: Five hits were predicted to occupy a significant space in the pocket flanked by TMs-II, III, and VII forming hydrophobic interactions, especially with residues Y281/2947.38 and Y285/2987.43, as previously found in the MT receptor structures (Johansson et al., 2019; Stauch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from the docking analysis supported by citations.

claim: Six of the identified hits were found to be at least 30 fold more potent at MT2 compared to MT1 in the Gi/o-mediated cAMP inhibition assays.
source: Six of the identified hits were found to be at least 30 fold more potent at MT2 compared to MT1 in the Gi/o-mediated cAMP inhibition assays.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental assays.

claim: Compound 21 was predicted to bind both the MT receptors in a similar orientation by forming hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60 and Q181/194ECL2 with its methoxy anchor and acetylamido tail, respectively.
source: Compound 21 was predicted to bind both the MT receptors in a similar orientation by forming hydrogen bonding interactions with N162/1754.60 and Q181/194ECL2 with its methoxy anchor and acetylamido tail, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the docking analysis.

claim: Compound 47 is 187-fold selective towards MT2 (EC50 = 10 nM for MT2, and 2.34 µM for MT1, respectively).
source: For example, compound 47 is 187-fold selective towards MT2 (EC50 = 10 nM for MT2, and 2.34 µM for MT1, respectively).
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 47.

claim: Compound 45 has a sub-micromolar potency and 17-fold selectivity for MT2 (EC50 = 427 nM).
source: Similarly, compound 45 also lacks a substitution topologically equivalent to acetylamido tail of melatonin (R2 feature) and yet has a sub-micromolar potency and 17-fold selectivity for MT2 (EC50 = 427 nM).
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 45.

claim: Compound 44 is 267-fold selective for MT2 (EC50 = 263 nM).
source: In contrast, compound 44 was predicted to form interactions with Q181/194ECL2, but it lacks an R3 equivalent substitution, which still makes it 267-fold selective for MT2 (EC50 = 263 nM).
evidence: This is an experimental result for compound 44.

claim: Either R2 or R3 could be sufficient in maintaining the potency and selectivity at MT2.
source: These findings suggest that either R2 or R3 could be sufficient in maintaining the potency and selectivity at MT2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and docking analysis.

claim: All the discovered hits show activity as agonists in Gi/o-protein signaling assays at both MT1 and MT2 receptors.
source: All the discovered hits show activity as agonists in Gi/o-protein signaling assays at both MT1 and MT2 receptors.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: Four of the hits, 28, 29, 57, and 62 had their efficacy (Emax) reduced to less than 70% in MT2, and are therefore considered partial agonists.
source: Thus, four of the hits, 28, 29, 57, and 62 had their efficacy (Emax) reduced to less than 70% in MT2, and are therefore considered partial agonists (Audinot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental assays.

claim: Compound 37 completely lacks G-protein signaling at MT1, though it still binds to MT1 and displays substantial β-arrestin activity.
source: One exception is compound 37, which completely lacks G-protein signaling, though it still binds to MT1 and displays substantial β-arrestin activity.
evidence: This is a result from the experimental assays.

claim: Compounds 21 and 28 show bias factors of 15.5 and 33.9, respectively, at MT2.
source: In the case of MT2, however, there are several compounds that show a marked reduction in β-arrestin signaling compared to G-protein, especially compounds 21 and 28, which show bias factors of 15.5 and 33.9, respectively (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental assays shown in Figure 5b.

claim: MT ligands may show rather distinct functional bias profiles in G-protein and β-arrestin signaling.
source: These results suggest that MT ligands may show rather distinct functional bias profiles in G-protein and β-arrestin signaling, as observed in many other GPCRs (Kenakin, 2019; Roth, 2019), though the biological importance of this bias in MT remains to be investigated (Cecon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results, supported by citations.

claim: Compound 28 is very similar to melatonin, except the amide is replaced by a urea.
source: Compound 28 is very similar to melatonin, except the amide is replaced by a urea.
evidence: This describes the chemical structure of compound 28.

claim: Compound 28 is a partial agonist at MT2 (Emax = 69.4%) while largely maintaining full agonism at MT1 (Emax = 95.3%).
source: This substitution renders compound 28 as a partial agonist at MT2 (Emax = 69.4%) while largely maintaining full agonism at MT1 (Emax = 95.3%).

claim: In MT2 orthosteric site, the urea of compound 28 forms hydrogen bonding interactions with the side chains of polar residues Q194ECL2 and N2686.52 owing to its additional nitrogen.
source: In MT2 orthosteric site, the urea of compound 28 forms hydrogen bonding interactions with the side chains of polar residues Q194ECL2 and N2686.52 owing to its additional nitrogen.

source: Instead, the interactions of acetylamido group of melatonin with Q181ECL2 are replaced by a hydrogen bond between Y2817.38 and oxygen from the urea in compound 28.

claim: The lead compounds 21, 28, and 37 did not show any substantial binding at 47 common drug targets at 10 μM, except for compound 28 that displayed over 50% inhibition at three 5-HT receptors.
source: At a final concentration of 10 μM, they did not show any substantial binding at these targets, except for compound 28 that displayed over 50% inhibition at three 5-HT receptors (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), with binding affinity of 851 nM (pKi = 6.07 ± 0.11) for 5-HT1A, 1525 nM (pKi = 5.82 ± 0.02) for 5-HT1D, and 286 nM (pKi = 6.54 ± 0.03) for 5-HT7A.
evidence: This is a result from the off-target profiling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Compound 28 has binding affinity of 851 nM (pKi = 6.07 ± 0.11) for 5-HT1A.
source: At a final concentration of 10 μM, they did not show any substantial binding at these targets, except for compound 28 that displayed over 50% inhibition at three 5-HT receptors (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), with binding affinity of 851 nM (pKi = 6.07 ± 0.11) for 5-HT1A, 1525 nM (pKi = 5.82 ± 0.02) for 5-HT1D, and 286 nM (pKi = 6.54 ± 0.03) for 5-HT7A.
evidence: This is a result from the off-target profiling.

claim: Compound 28 has binding affinity of 1525 nM (pKi = 5.82 ± 0.02) for 5-HT1D.
source: At a final concentration of 10 μM, they did not show any substantial binding at these targets, except for compound 28 that displayed over 50% inhibition at three 5-HT receptors (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), with binding affinity of 851 nM (pKi = 6.07 ± 0.11) for 5-HT1A, 1525 nM (pKi = 5.82 ± 0.02) for 5-HT1D, and 286 nM (pKi = 6.54 ± 0.03) for 5-HT7A.
evidence: This is a result from the off-target profiling.

claim: Compound 28 has binding affinity of 286 nM (pKi = 6.54 ± 0.03) for 5-HT7A.
source: At a final concentration of 10 μM, they did not show any substantial binding at these targets, except for compound 28 that displayed over 50% inhibition at three 5-HT receptors (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), with binding affinity of 851 nM (pKi = 6.07 ± 0.11) for 5-HT1A, 1525 nM (pKi = 5.82 ± 0.02) for 5-HT1D, and 286 nM (pKi = 6.54 ± 0.03) for 5-HT7A.
evidence: This is a result from the off-target profiling.

claim: Compound 28 is a weak partial agonist at 5-HT7A with EC50 = 1819 nM, as compared to 0.04 nM at both MT1 and MT2 receptors.
source: Assessment of functional activity of 28 in Gs-mediated cAMP production shows that it is a weak partial agonist with EC50 = 1819 nM, as compared to 0.04 nM at both MT1 and MT2 receptors.
evidence: This is a result from the functional assays.

claim: The lead compounds 21, 28, and 37 act specifically at MT receptors and show high selectivity for MT1 or MT2 over many common drug targets.
source: These results demonstrated that the lead compounds 21, 28, and 37 act specifically at MT receptors and show high selectivity for MT1 or MT2 over many common drug targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the off-target profiling results.

claim: The number of sub-micromolar hits and potency of the best among them is one of the highest reported for a VLS campaign in class A GPCRs.
source: The number of sub-micromolar hits and potency of the best among them is one of the highest reported for a VLS campaign in class A GPCRs (Lyu et al., 2019) and in-line with another VLS screen for MT receptors, published while this study was in revision (Stein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to other VLS campaigns, supported by citations.

claim: Most GPCR structures have a limited capacity to distinguish agonists vs. antagonists.
source: This is remarkable, considering that most GPCR structures have a limited capacity to distinguish agonists vs. antagonists (Costanzi and Vilar, 2012; Weiss et al., 2018) and prospective VLS campaigns often result in antagonists even when an agonist-bound VLS model is used (Lyu et al., 2019; Roth, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Prospective VLS campaigns often result in antagonists even when an agonist-bound VLS model is used.
source: This is remarkable, considering that most GPCR structures have a limited capacity to distinguish agonists vs. antagonists (Costanzi and Vilar, 2012; Weiss et al., 2018) and prospective VLS campaigns often result in antagonists even when an agonist-bound VLS model is used (Lyu et al., 2019; Roth, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The high quality of the initial crystal structure, further improved by ligand-guided optimization of the pocket for VLS, has been critical for the success of previous VLS campaigns.
source: Thus, the high quality of the initial crystal structure, further improved by ligand-guided optimization of the pocket for VLS, has been critical for the success of our previous VLS campaigns, and likely played a similar role here (Katritch et al., 2010; Lane et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Endogenous ligand melatonin has unusually high picomolar potency at MT receptors (~4 pM at MT1 and 50 pM at MT2).
source: As we mentioned above, endogenous ligand melatonin itself has unusually high picomolar potency at MT receptors (~4 pM at MT1 and 50 pM at MT2, see Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental assays shown in Table 1.

claim: Melatonin and most other high-potency ligands are small (<250 DA) and yet they still fully occupy the very small, enclosed MT pocket.
source: Melatonin and most other high-potency ligands are small (<250 DA) and yet they still fully occupy the very small, enclosed MT pocket.
evidence: This is an observation about the properties of MT ligands.

claim: Chemical space of fragment-like libraries is much smaller than the usual drug-like space, and can be more exhaustively searched, likely resulting in higher hit rates.
source: Chemical space of such size-limited fragment-like libraries is much smaller than the usual drug-like space, and can be more exhaustively searched, likely resulting in higher hit rates.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of fragment-like libraries.

claim: Most known MT receptor ligands show agonist activity, while antagonists of similar potency are notoriously hard to find.
source: Moreover, most known MT receptor ligands show agonist activity, while antagonists of similar potency are notoriously hard to find, suggesting that agonists may be intrinsically preferred ligands for MT receptors (Jockers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Agonists may be intrinsically preferred ligands for MT receptors.
source: Moreover, most known MT receptor ligands show agonist activity, while antagonists of similar potency are notoriously hard to find, suggesting that agonists may be intrinsically preferred ligands for MT receptors (Jockers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Two of the hit compounds, 37 and 62, are MT2-selective partial agonists.
source: Two of the hit compounds, 37 and 62, are MT2-selective partial agonists, which may have a desirable profile for eliciting antinociceptive effects mediated by melatonin receptors, and may be potentially useful in developing novel analgesics for pain management with reduced side effects (López-Canul et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental assays.

claim: MT2-selective partial agonists may have a desirable profile for eliciting antinociceptive effects mediated by melatonin receptors.
source: Two of the hit compounds, 37 and 62, are MT2-selective partial agonists, which may have a desirable profile for eliciting antinociceptive effects mediated by melatonin receptors, and may be potentially useful in developing novel analgesics for pain management with reduced side effects (López-Canul et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: None of the hits in this study had substantial MT1 selectivity.
source: Of note, while some of the newly discovered hits are selective for MT2, none of the hits in this study had substantial MT1 selectivity.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: The lack of MT1 selectivity may be explained by the lack of a bulky chemical group at the R1 position.
source: This may be explained by the lack of a bulky chemical group at the R1 position, which are known to confer strong MT1 selectivity, e.g. in bitopic CTL 01–05-B-A05 ligand that stretches out of the pocket via narrow side channel (Stauch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Design of bitopic ligands with MT1 selective chemotypes would need to explore larger compounds (MW >500).
source: Design of such bitopic ligands with MT1 selective chemotypes would need to explore larger compounds (MW >500), which were not considered in the current VLS screen.
evidence: This is a speculation about future work.

claim: Prevalence of agonists in the hit set suggests the importance of activated, agonist-bound conformations of the orthosteric pocket models for successful agonist screening.
source: Prevalence of agonists in the hit set suggests the importance of activated, agonist-bound conformations of the orthosteric pocket models for successful agonist screening.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Even though the receptors were thermostabilized by 9 and 8 point mutations (MT1/MT2, respectively) to aid crystallization rendering the receptor conformations inactive on the intracellular side, the agonist-bound orthosteric pockets remain relevant for structure-based drug discovery applications.
source: Note that, even though the receptors were thermostabilized by 9 and 8 point mutations (MT1/MT2, respectively) to aid crystallization rendering the receptor conformations inactive on the intracellular side, the agonist-bound orthosteric pockets remain relevant for structure-based drug discovery applications.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful VLS results.

claim: Ligand guided receptor optimization (LiBERO) plays an important role in improving the outcomes of a structure-based VLS.
source: Our benchmarking also corroborated the important role of ligand guided receptor optimization (LiBERO) (Katritch et al., 2012) in improving the outcomes of a structure-based VLS, similar to some of our previous VLS campaigns (Lane et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the benchmarking results and citations to prior work.

claim: The chemical diversity, selectivity, high potency and agonist activities of the identified hits serve as a valuable starting point for the development of tool compounds to explore the biology of melatonin receptors.
source: The chemical diversity, selectivity, high potency and agonist activities of the identified hits serve as a valuable starting point for the development of tool compounds to explore the biology of melatonin receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential utility of the hits.

claim: These novel chemotypes could provide new leads for the development of next-generation treatments for insomnia, pain, sleep and mood-related disorders, type 2 diabetes, and cancer.
source: With the potential for selective modulation over the melatonin receptor subtype-mediated biology, these novel chemotypes could provide new leads for the development of next-generation treatments for insomnia, pain, sleep and mood-related disorders, type 2 diabetes, and cancer.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential therapeutic applications.

claim: X-ray crystal structures of MT1 and MT2 receptors in complex with 2-phenylmelatonin (PDB IDs: 6ME3, 6ME6) were used to generate virtual screening models.
source: X-ray crystal structures of MT1 (Stauch et al., 2019) and MT2 (Johansson et al., 2019) receptors in complex with 2-phenylmelatonin (PDB IDs Berman et al., 2000: 6ME3, 6ME6) were used to generate virtual screening models.
evidence: This describes the starting materials for the modeling work.

claim: The RMSD values of ligand binding pocket side chain heavy atoms for MT1 and MT2 were 0.51 Å and 0.76 Å, respectively, compared to their corresponding crystal structures.
source: The RMSD values of ligand binding pocket side chain heavy atoms for MT1 and MT2 were 0.51 Å and 0.76 Å, respectively, compared to their corresponding crystal structures.
evidence: This is a result from the receptor model optimization.

claim: A subset of commercially available fragment-like compounds from the ZINC database with physicochemical properties similar to already reported melatonin receptor ligands was selected for screening.
source: We selected a subset of commercially available (in-stock and on-demand) fragment-like compounds from the ZINC database with physicochemical properties similar to already reported melatonin receptor ligands (Gaulton et al., 2017; Sterling and Irwin, 2015).
evidence: This describes the screening library selection criteria.

claim: Compounds with molecular weight ≤250 Da and logP values ranging 1 to 5 were considered for the screening library.
source: We considered compounds with molecular weight ≤250 Da and logP values ranging 1 to 5 based on the logP data of high-affinity MT ligands (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the screening library selection criteria.

claim: The initial dataset comprised of ~10 million compounds was converted from SMILES to 3D format, and formal charges were assigned.
source: The initial dataset comprised of ~10 million compounds was converted from SMILES to 3D format, and formal charges were assigned.
evidence: This describes the library preparation process.

claim: The dataset was reduced to 8.4 million compounds after applying additional filters for net charges (between −1 to 1) and removing compounds with highly reactive functional groups and promiscuous PAINS chemotypes.
source: This set was further reduced to 8.4 million compounds after applying additional filters for net charges (between −1 to 1) and removing compounds with highly reactive functional groups and promiscuous PAINS chemotypes ('molPAINS' and 'bad groups' in ICM-Pro v.3.8–6) (Baell and Holloway, 2010).
evidence: This describes the library preparation process.

claim: All compounds for in vitro testing were purchased from Enamine, Molport, and Chembridge in stock libraries, with verified identity and guaranteed purity of >95% (37 compounds) or >90% (25 compounds).
source: All compounds for in vitro testing were purchased from Enamine, Molport, and Chembridge in stock libraries, with verified identity and guaranteed purity of >95% (37 compounds) or >90% (25 compounds), see Supplementary file 2 for compound QC data).
evidence: This describes the quality of the compounds tested.

claim: Radioligand binding assays were conducted by the NIMH Psychoactive Drug Screening Program (PDSP).
source: The Radioligand binding assays were conducted by the NIMH Psychoactive Drug Screening Program (PDSP).
evidence: This describes who performed the binding assays.

claim: [3H]melatonin (PerkinElmer, specific activity = 77.4–84.7 Ci/mmol) is used as the radioligand in binding assays.
source: [3H]melatonin (PerkinElmer, specific activity = 77.4–84.7 Ci/mmol) is used as the radioligand.
evidence: This describes the radioligand used in the binding assays.

claim: Bias factors were estimated according to the published procedure with modifications.
source: Bias factors were estimated according to the published procedure Kenakin et al. (2012) with modifications.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating bias factors.
